title: Reasor-Hill Corp. v. Harrison (1952)
summary: Arkansas allowed a damages claim concerning injury to Missouri land rather than applying the traditional local-action bar.
notes:
The syllabus cites page 395, the beginning of the chapter; the case itself begins at printed page 399. Later federal venue reforms discussed in the chapter should be kept distinct from this state-court decision.

The suit began when Planters Flying Service sued D.M. Barton in Arkansas for crop-spraying fees; Barton answered that the spraying had ruined his Missouri cotton crop and cross-complained against the insecticide's manufacturer, Reasor-Hill, which then petitioned the Arkansas Supreme Court for a writ to stop the trial court from hearing the cross-complaint.

sections.Parties: Reasor-Hill, an Arkansas chemical manufacturer, sought to prevent the Arkansas court from hearing a claim arising from alleged damage to crops in Missouri. Harrison was the respondent judge in the prohibition proceeding.
sections.Material Facts: The litigation involved chemicals alleged to have damaged crops on Missouri land. The manufacturer could be reached in Arkansas, but obtaining jurisdiction over it in Missouri posed a practical problem. The contested claim sought personal monetary relief for the alleged injury. It did not require Arkansas to transfer title to Missouri real estate or exercise physical control over that property.
sections.Procedural History: The manufacturer sought a writ of prohibition against the Arkansas trial judge. The Arkansas Supreme Court denied the writ and declined to apply the older rule that would confine the action to the place where the land lay.
sections.Issue: Should an Arkansas court refuse to hear a personal damages claim solely because the alleged injury concerned land in another state?
sections.Holding: No. The court allowed the damages action to proceed and rejected the traditional bar in the circumstances presented.
sections.Reasoning: The court examined the historical local-action rule critically rather than treating its pedigree as sufficient justification. Applying it could leave a claimant without an effective forum despite the defendant’s availability in Arkansas. A damages judgment directed at a defendant differs from a decree directly determining ownership of foreign land. The court considered that difference important to whether territorial limits required dismissal. The decision also reflects disagreement over whether courts or legislatures should change inherited procedural rules.

learning.why: Arkansas allowed a damages claim concerning injury to Missouri land rather than applying the traditional local-action bar.

topics.cp-local-actions: The state court rejected a territorial bar to an action for injury to out-of-state land.
topics.cp-venue: The local-action tradition could prevent a remedy even where the defendant was reachable in the chosen forum.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: A claim for damages for injury to land was distinguished from an adjudication determining title to the land.
topics.cp-personal-jurisdiction: The court's key practical concern was that Missouri had no way to obtain jurisdiction over the Arkansas manufacturer, so applying the local-action rule would leave the plaintiff without a forum.

learning.separateOpinions: The dissent favored adherence to the established local-action rule and regarded a change as a legislative matter.
